description: Somos Jorge Ainaga, Marta Alba, Blanca Pérez, Felipe Blasco y Rodolfo Callejas, ingenieros formados en la EINA, nos apasionan los retos y sobre todo aquellos que tratamos de resolver juntos.
summary: Field Shift is a web decision-support tool that helps farmers explore crop and rotation options for their own field using NASA Earth observations. Farmers pick a real field on the map or draw one, and the tool builds a traceable profile from NASA POWER climate (frost, heat stress, FAO-56 evapotranspiration, water balance, extreme rain), SMAP root-zone moisture, Landsat NDVI/NDTI (months with bare soil), NASADEM slope with erosion and frost-pocket risk zones, plus USDA soil and the field's crop history. It screens 15 crops with transparent agronomic rules (heat to mature, water need, heat at flowering, frost, winter cold, soil pH), ranks them as recommended, possible with care or not recommended, and proposes a 4-season legume-cereal rotation that cuts nitrogen fertiliser. A scenario simulator lets farmers test drier, hotter conditions and irrigation and instantly see the effect on each crop, and a money check gives costs, break-even and lower-yield cases. Every value shows its source, resolution and confidence in plain language. As the climate shifts, farmers need evidence-based ways to adapt; Field Shift turns complex satellite data into clear, honest guidance that supports, not replaces, their judgment.
details:
What it does and how it works

Field Shift is a web decision-support tool. It helps a farmer answer three questions about one specific field: what can I grow here, how should I rotate it, and what happens if the climate gets hotter or drier?

  1. Pick the field. On the map, the farmer zooms in and clicks a real field outline from the USDA Crop Sequence Boundaries. They can also draw the field by clicking its corners, or open one of the demo fields.
    • NASA POWER (daily, 10 years): frost dates, heat-stress days, reference evapotranspiration computed with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method, monthly water balance (rain minus ET0) and extreme-rain indices (R95p, R20mm, Rx1day).
    • SMAP L4: root-zone soil moisture and its anomalies.
    • Landsat 8/9: NDVI (green vigour) and NDTI (crop residue), used to find the months when the field usually lies bare.
    • NASADEM: slope at 30 m, a relative erosion-risk index and possible cold-air pooling zones (frost pockets).
    • Soil (USDA SSURGO or OpenLandMap): pH, texture, clay, sand, organic carbon and field capacity.
    • Crop history (USDA Cropland Data Layer): what was grown on the field each year, which tells us the current rotation.
  2. Screen the crops. Each of 15 crops in the catalogue is checked against the field: enough heat to mature (growing degree-days), enough water (crop need from Kc × ET0 against rain plus stored soil water, with FAO-33 yield-loss logic), heat at flowering, a long enough frost-free season, frost risk at sowing, winter cold, vernalization, humidity and disease risk, soil pH and texture. Each crop ends up as recommended, possible with care or not recommended, and every check gives its reason in plain words with the numbers underneath.
  3. Propose a rotation. Starting from the last crop grown on the field, the tool builds a 4-season plan that alternates a nitrogen-fixing legume (soybean, peanut) with a crop that uses nitrogen (corn, wheat, sorghum, cotton…). It only uses crops that passed the screening, and it prefers crops the farmer already grows. It estimates the nitrogen fertiliser saved and offers alfalfa as an alternative legume phase. If no legume fits, it suggests a winter legume cover crop.
  4. Simulate scenarios. Sliders lower rainfall (down to −30 %), raise temperature (up to +3 °C) and add hypothetical irrigation. The simulator applies these changes to the field's real NASA daily series and re-runs the same calculations, so the farmer sees in under 200 ms how each crop's checks move from ok to tight to limiting. With every slider at zero, the result matches the base analysis exactly, and a test checks this.
  5. Check the money. For the chosen crop, the tool computes total cost, expected income, cash available, break-even yield and price, and a what-if table for yields 10, 20 and 30 % lower. The defaults come from Iowa State University 2026 budgets, USDA ERS cost forecasts and USDA WASDE prices, and the farmer can edit any of them.
  6. See it on the map. A Leaflet viewer shows NDVI, root-zone moisture, rainfall, slope and risk zones, each drawn at its real resolution. A cursor inspector says "value of the ~9 km zone" for coarse data, never "value at this point".

Benefits

  • Specific to one field: every answer is about the farmer's own field, not about a county average.
  • Explainable: no black-box score. Every verdict shows the rule, the threshold, the number and the source, first in plain language and then in figures.
  • Honest about uncertainty: every indicator carries its source, whether it is NASA data, its data type (satellite, model, reanalysis), its real resolution, a confidence level with the reason, and any data gaps.
  • Shows the trade-offs: farmers can test how a drier, hotter season changes their options before committing seed and money.
  • Builds soil health: the rotation logic rewards legumes, cuts the need for nitrogen fertiliser, breaks up monocultures and points out bare-soil months and erosion-prone slopes.
  • Easy to run: one command starts it. It works without any account using NASA POWER, USDA SSURGO and USDA CropScape. Google Earth Engine is an optional extra.

Intended impact

Climate change is shifting frost dates, heat extremes and rainfall patterns faster than traditional local knowledge can adjust. Farmers rarely have the time or training to turn satellite data into decisions. Field Shift aims to:

  • give farmers a free, transparent first screening of their adaptation options;
  • encourage diversified rotations that protect soil, save water and reduce fertiliser costs;
  • start better-informed conversations between farmers, agronomists and extension services.

The tool supports the farmer's judgment and never replaces it. Every scenario carries the label "Hypothetical scenario, not a prediction", and the limits of each dataset are always visible.

Tools, languages and software

  • Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Pydantic and the Google Earth Engine Python API.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with Leaflet 1.9.4 for maps and Chart.js 4.4.1 for charts.
  • Data and APIs: NASA POWER (daily API, AG community), SMAP L4 (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008), Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level-2, NASADEM, Copernicus DEM (fallback), OpenLandMap, USDA SSURGO (Soil Data Access), USDA Cropland Data Layer and CropScape, USDA Crop Sequence Boundaries, OpenStreetMap (Overpass and Nominatim) and Esri World Imagery as the basemap.
  • Scientific methods: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith and Hargreaves-Samani ET0, FAO-33 yield response to water, growing degree-days (McMaster & Wilhelm), heat thresholds from Hatfield et al. (2011), ETCCDI extreme-rain indices, NDTI (Van Deventer et al.) and USDA hardiness zones.
  • Quality: pytest unit tests check the formulas against FAO-56 worked examples. Smoke tests run against the live APIs. A validation script compares the crop screening with what USDA NASS reports is actually grown at 10 US reference sites.
  • Hardware: team laptops (Windows). No special hardware is needed.
  • AI assistance: most of the code was written with an AI coding assistant (Claude). The team chose the concept, the scope, the datasets and the method, and reviewed the code. This is declared in the README, in every Python file header and in each API response (provenance.ai_assistance).

What makes it creative

  • Climate futures on the farmer's own data. Instead of a generic climate projection, the simulator shifts the field's own 10-year NASA daily record. The farmer sees "your last 10 years, but 2 °C hotter and 20 % drier".
  • Honesty built into the output. NDVI is labelled "green vigour", not fertility or yield. The SMAP and POWER wetness values are labelled as indices, not volumetric moisture. The erosion index is relative, never shown in t/ha/yr. The vulnerability indicator is labelled as co-occurrence, not causation.
  • Mixed resolutions shown, not hidden. A 30 m slope pixel, a 9 km SMAP cell and a 50 km POWER cell each appear on the map at their true footprint, so the farmer can see how local each number really is.
  • Tested against real farms. At the 10 US reference sites, the first version wrongly rejected 29 commercial crops and wrongly passed 11 crops that cannot grow there. After the revision it gets 0 and 1 wrong. Each catalogue value we corrected is recorded with the old value and the reason.
  • Plain language first. Every check has a one-line explanation in everyday words, with the numbers behind it one click away.

What the team considered

  • Farmer priorities and constraints: available water (hypothetical irrigation), what is already grown on the field, nitrogen, erosion, bare soil and money available.
  • Scale and resolution: we never present a zone value as a point value, and we state the scale for each layer.
  • Data availability and access: fallbacks that need no login, so the tool works without Earth Engine; a cache and precomputed demo fields to stay within the Earth Engine Community quota (150 EECU-hours a month).
  • Scientific integrity: sourced parameters, thresholds tagged as standard or as team hypothesis, and no invented yields, probabilities or prices presented as forecasts.
  • Licences and attribution: NASA POWER citation text, CC-BY-SA for OpenLandMap, ODbL for OpenStreetMap, and Esri attribution on the map.
  • Responsible use of AI: full disclosure, and AI was never used as a data source. Every number comes from a cited dataset or formula.
  • Limits stated openly: about 50 km climate cells smooth out valley frost and local rain, the crop screening is rule-based and does not forecast yields, and the tool currently covers US crops and datasets.
